docs.text: This section documents the Doly Python SDK.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Doly Python SDK is a collection of small, focused modules (one per capability) built on top of Doly’s C++ SDK using pybind11.

  • Platform: Raspberry Pi OS
  • Python: 3.11
  • Distribution: preinstalled on the robot; developers can rebuild modules from source.

docs.title: Python API reference
docs.text: Reference for the current Python module families. These pages describe the maintained Python interfaces, including adapters, properties and callback helpers.

docs.title: Signatures and return values
docs.text:
Use the Python names and defaults on each page. A native integer status, Python exception, boolean result and None are different contracts. Check the documented status before using tuple payloads. In particular, Drive disposal returns None, and Helper/IMU calibration adapters return a status followed by six offsets.

Callable and Optional in signatures describe Python callables and values that may be None; they are typing notation, not SDK classes. Listener method parameter names describe positional event payloads unless keyword support is explicitly documented. Native integer parameters have their native signed/unsigned width; out-of-range or incompatible arguments can fail Python conversion rather than returning a native error status. Only explicitly documented adapters clamp inputs.

Shared types have one owner: Position in doly_helper, Color in doly_color, GpioState in doly_io, and VContent in doly_vcontent. Other modules reuse these types. Do not construct unexposed native types or call native destructors directly.

docs.title: Callbacks and listeners
docs.text:
add_listener(listener, priority=False) accepts the component's listener type. add_listener(None) does nothing. The wrapper retains registered Python targets; dropping an application reference does not unregister a listener. Drive and Battery deduplicate the same object. Other callback components permit duplicate object registrations. remove_listener(listener) removes one matching registration: the newest priority registration first, otherwise the oldest normal registration.

Within one event dispatch, priority object listeners run first, newest priority registration first. Normal object listeners follow in registration order. This does not establish ordering between separate events.

Each on_* setter accepts one callable or None. A callable installs or replaces that event's function callback; None removes it. Noncallable values raise TypeError. Most setters use keyword cb; Battery uses callback. Object listeners are dispatched before function callbacks in native event ordering. Callbacks run through native dispatch with the Python GIL, not through an application event queue. Exceptions from callbacks are reported as unraisable and do not escape into native event dispatch. Keep callbacks short and schedule blocking control work on the application control thread.

clear_listeners() removes both object and function registrations for that component. It does not dispose hardware or wait for callbacks to drain. Edge also provides clear_callbacks(), which removes only function callbacks. Explicit removal and self-removal do not wait for already executing callbacks to finish; native registry removal may briefly acquire its own mutex.

An event admitted before a function callback is removed can reach its replacement after re-registration. Removing and re-registering a function callback does not isolate old events from new handlers. For frequent replacement, prefer class-based listeners. An already executing callback may still finish; class listeners do not provide a complete shutdown or drainage guarantee.

docs.title: Initialization and disposal
docs.text:
Use each component's existing dispose() on the application control thread before interpreter finalization. There is no public global callback shutdown function and no doly_helper.close_callbacks(). Callback cleanup affects only that component; Drive's native dispose_IMU option does not clear Python IMU registrations.

Initialization and blocking operations identified on each page raise RuntimeError when called from any wrapper callback. Disposal adapters with known rejection codes return those codes instead. Drive preserves its None adapter; Eye performs only callback cleanup. New registration during disposal/finalization raises RuntimeError.

Disposal pauses callback admission. Suppressed events are not queued or replayed. Rejected native disposal retains surviving registration identities, priorities, ordering and Python targets. Explicit removals made during the attempt stay removed. Accepted cleanup unregisters that component and releases Python target references after admitted Python entries finish. An executing callback holds a local target reference. Native disposal can block indefinitely; a status does not universally prove native worker drainage.

Each newly created object registration retains a native proxy until process termination, even after accepted cleanup. Removing and registering again creates another retained proxy; no reclamation or bounded-memory guarantee is made. add_listener(None) and ignored duplicate registrations in Battery/Drive return before allocation. Function callback setters reuse one subscription per event. Ambiguous Sound/IMU failures may retain Python targets until explicit removal or later accepted disposal.

docs.title: Ownership and limitations
docs.text:
Camera owns its options; returned frames own their Python array storage. VContent shares native ownership with Eye, which retains final image owners because no supported detach-and-join API exists. LCD retains exported buffers through synchronous native access. Follow the image dimensions, idle-state, initialization and buffer requirements on those pages. Do not operate LCD and Eye concurrently.

Wrapper coordination does not synchronize external C++ callers or repair native rendering/shutdown races. Interpreter exit does not dispose native devices or guarantee safe shutdown; dispose components on the control thread before finalization. Embedded interpreter restart, subinterpreters, free-threaded Python, dynamic unloading and native entry into Python during finalization are unsupported. See installation and compatibility for interpreter and platform requirements.

docs.title: Usage demonstrations
docs.text: Each component API page links to its module guide, which includes the full example and its source path under examples/python/ in the SDK distribution. Color and VContent refer to the LED/Eye guides. Follow each guide's device, asset, and cleanup requirements. The Battery example is for reading only and must never execute.

docs.title: ArmEventListener
docs.text:
ArmEventListener() constructs the listener base. Subclass it and register it with add_listener() to receive events.

Methods

  • onArmComplete(id: int, side: ArmSide) -> None
  • Called when an arm command completes successfully.
  • onArmError(id: int, side: ArmSide, error_type: ArmErrorType) -> None
  • Called when an arm command ends with an error.
  • onArmStateChange(side: ArmSide, state: ArmState) -> None
  • Called when the arm state changes.
  • onArmMovement(side: ArmSide, degree_change: float) -> None
  • Called to report incremental motion events.

docs.title: add_listener(listener: Optional[ArmEventListener], priority: bool = False) -> None
docs.text:
Register a listener object to receive events. None does nothing. The wrapper retains the Python target until removal, clearing or accepted disposal.

  • listener: An instance of ArmEventListener or a subclass, or None.
  • priority: Insert with priority ordering (default False).

Duplicate object registrations are permitted; each has a distinct native proxy. See callback ordering and lifetime.

docs.title: remove_listener(listener: ArmEventListener) -> None
docs.text: Unregister one matching object registration. listener is the Python object previously passed to add_listener(). For duplicates, the newest priority registration is removed first, otherwise the oldest normal registration. Removal does not wait for already executing callbacks to finish.

docs.title: on_complete(cb: Optional[Callable[[int, ArmSide], None]]) -> None
docs.text:
Set the complete function callback, replacing any previous callable.

  • cb: Called as cb(id, side); pass None to unregister this function callback. It returns None. A noncallable, non-None value raises TypeError.

For multiple handlers, use class-based listeners or an application dispatcher. See delayed-callback and exception behavior.

docs.title: on_error(cb: Optional[Callable[[int, ArmSide, ArmErrorType], None]]) -> None
docs.text:
Set the error function callback, replacing any previous callable.

  • cb: Called as cb(id, side, error_type); pass None to unregister this function callback. It returns None. A noncallable, non-None value raises TypeError.

For multiple handlers, use class-based listeners or an application dispatcher. See delayed-callback and exception behavior.

docs.title: on_state_change(cb: Optional[Callable[[ArmSide, ArmState], None]]) -> None
docs.text:
Set the state change function callback, replacing any previous callable.

  • cb: Called as cb(side, state); pass None to unregister this function callback. It returns None. A noncallable, non-None value raises TypeError.

For multiple handlers, use class-based listeners or an application dispatcher. See delayed-callback and exception behavior.

docs.title: on_movement(cb: Optional[Callable[[ArmSide, float], None]]) -> None
docs.text:
Set the movement function callback, replacing any previous callable.

  • cb: Called as cb(side, degree_change); pass None to unregister this function callback. It returns None. A noncallable, non-None value raises TypeError.

For multiple handlers, use class-based listeners or an application dispatcher. See delayed-callback and exception behavior.

docs.title: clear_listeners() -> None
docs.text: Unregister all object listeners and function callbacks belonging to this component and release their stored Python targets. This does not dispose hardware or wait for callback drainage. Already executing callbacks may finish.

docs.title: init() -> int
docs.text:
Initialize the arm subsystem.

This must be called once before other control functions.

Returns

  • int:
0: success
1: already initialized
-1: left servo enable pin failed
-2: right servo enable pin failed
-3: ServoMotor initialization failed
-4: channel setup failed
-5: initial release failed

Notes

  • After successful init(), is_active() should return true.

docs.title: dispose() -> int
docs.text:
Dispose/stop the arm subsystem and release resources. Accepted disposal also cleans up Arm Python callbacks; rejection retains registrations.

Returns

  • int:
0: success
1: not initialized
-3: callback-context rejection; registrations retained
-5: resource release error after teardown; Python callback cleanup accepted

docs.title: is_active() -> bool
docs.text:
Check whether the subsystem is active (initialized and running).

Returns

  • bool:
true if active, false otherwise.

docs.title: abort(side: ArmSide) -> None
docs.text:
Abort the current operation for a given side.

This is intended as an emergency/stop action.

Parameters

  • side: Arm side to abort (ArmSide.Left/ArmSide.Right/ArmSide.Both).

docs.title: get_max_angle() -> int
docs.text:
Get maximum allowed angle for the arm.

Returns

  • int:
Maximum angle (degrees).

docs.title: set_angle(id: int, side: ArmSide, speed: int, angle: int, with_brake: bool = False) -> int
docs.text:
Command the arm to move to an angle.

Motion runs asynchronously, but command submission may wait for previous work or motor readiness. A zero result means the command was accepted, not completed. Use state and ArmEventListener.onArmComplete(), onArmError(), and onArmStateChange() to observe the outcome.

Parameters

  • id: User-defined command identifier (echoed back in completion/error callbacks).
  • side: Arm side to move (ArmSide.Left/ArmSide.Right/ArmSide.Both).
  • speed: Speed percentage in range [1..100].
  • angle: Target angle in degrees in range [0..get_max_angle()].
  • with_brake: If True, apply brake/hold behavior at target (implementation-defined). (default: False)

Returns

  • int:
0: command accepted
-1: controller inactive or lower-level motor angle failure
-2: speed or lower-level motor parameter/channel failure
-3: angle/side validation or motor availability failure
-4: movement worker could not start

Motion error codes can overlap between controller validation and forwarded motor failures; a code does not uniquely identify the cause.

docs.title: get_state(side: ArmSide) -> ArmState
docs.text:
Get current operation state for a side.

Parameters

  • side: Arm side.

Returns

  • ArmState:
Current ArmState.

docs.title: get_current_angle(side: ArmSide) -> list[ArmData]
docs.text:
Get the current angle(s) for the requested side(s).

Parameters

  • side: Requested side (ArmSide.Left/ArmSide.Right/ArmSide.Both).

Returns

  • list[ArmData]:
List of ArmData entries. If side == ArmSide.Both, the list may contain 2 elements.

docs.title: get_version() -> float
docs.text:
Get SDK/library version.

Format note from original header: 0.XYZ (3 digits after major).

Returns

  • float:
Version as float.

docs.title: Lifecycle contract
docs.text:
init() and abort(side) raise RuntimeError from any wrapper callback. dispose() instead returns -3 there. Call lifecycle operations on the control thread. Disposal outcomes 0, 1 and -5 accept Python callback cleanup; a negative status must still be reported as an operation failure.

See initialization and disposal for component-local cleanup, retained native proxies and interpreter limitations.

docs.title: BatteryControl API reference
docs.text:
Import:

import doly_battery

This page documents the public API exposed by the doly_battery Python module: battery monitoring, capacity and alarm callbacks. Initialize monitoring before using readings. Capacity is an estimate in percent, not a measurement of true state of charge or a calibration guarantee.

docs.title: BatteryEventListener
docs.text:
BatteryEventListener() constructs the listener base. Subclass it and register the instance with add_listener() to receive alarms.

Methods

  • on_battery_alarm(capacity: int) -> None
  • Called with capacity in percent when the battery alarm is delivered. The bound method supports the keyword capacity.

The proxy also recognizes a legacy Python onBatteryAlarm override. Override-name selection occurs once at registration. This is not an additional bound base-class method; prefer on_battery_alarm in new subclasses.

docs.title: add_listener(listener: Optional[BatteryEventListener], priority: bool = False) -> None
docs.text:
Register a listener instance. The wrapper retains its Python target until removal, clearing or accepted component disposal. None does nothing. Registering the same object again is ignored; it does not change the original registration's priority.

  • listener: A BatteryEventListener instance/subclass, or None.
  • priority: Insert with priority ordering, default False.

docs.title: remove_listener(listener: Optional[BatteryEventListener]) -> None
docs.text: Unregister the given listener object. None does nothing. Removal does not wait for an already executing callback to finish.

docs.title: on_alarm(callback: Optional[Callable[[int], None]]) -> None
docs.text:
Install or replace the single alarm function callback. It is called as callback(capacity) and returns None. Pass None to unregister it. The keyword is callback, not cb; a noncallable, non-None value raises TypeError.

See callback ordering, exceptions and delayed delivery.

docs.title: clear_listeners() -> None
docs.text: Unregister this component's object listeners and function callback and release their stored Python targets. This neither disposes battery monitoring nor waits for callback drainage. An already executing callback may finish.

docs.title: init() -> int
docs.text:
Initialize battery monitoring.

Returns

0: success
1: already active or lifecycle operation in progress
-1: sensor path unavailable

From any wrapper callback this raises RuntimeError; initialize on the application control thread.

docs.title: dispose() -> int
docs.text:
Dispose battery monitoring and release resources. Native 0/1 permit cleanup of Battery Python subscriptions. Native -1 retains surviving registrations.

Returns

0: success
1: already inactive, including after waiting for another disposal to complete
-1: rejected disposal, including callback context; registrations retained

Call on the application control thread. Accepted Python cleanup is not proof of universal native drainage or bounded disposal time.

docs.title: is_active() -> bool
docs.text: Return whether battery monitoring is initialized and active.

docs.title: set_alarm_threshold(value: int) -> None
docs.text:
An alarm may be delivered when the capacity estimate is below the configured threshold (capacity < threshold). The native alarm repeat interval is ten seconds. This does not guarantee that an event will occur during a particular observation period.

value is forwarded as an unsigned 8-bit integer (0–255). Use 0–100 for an ordinary percentage threshold. The wrapper does not clamp values to 0–100; values outside the native integer range fail conversion.

docs.title: get_capacity() -> int
docs.text: Return the current capacity estimate in percent. Read after successful initialization. The reported 0–100 estimate does not establish physical current accuracy, sensor calibration or true state of charge.

docs.title: get_version() -> float
docs.text: Return the current library version as a float.

docs.title: Lifecycle and supported scope
docs.text:
See initialization and disposal for registration rejection during disposal, callback target retention, resident proxy shells and interpreter limitations. Native initialization rollback, unchecked sensor reads, retained filter/status state and potentially blocking disposal remain limitations; the Python interface does not establish complete lifecycle safety.

BatteryStatus, status callbacks/delivery, get_status, get_charge_time, current/voltage readings and internal event lifecycle/dispatch functions are not exposed Python features.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Obtain this object from camera.options on a PiCamera instance. There is no standalone Python Options() constructor. The options reference retains its owning camera; the options property cannot be replaced, but the fields below are writable. Configure options before starting the corresponding capture mode.

Fields

  • help: bool
  • version: bool
  • list_cameras: bool
  • verbose: bool
  • timeout: int
  • photo_width: int
  • photo_height: int
  • video_width: int
  • video_height: int
  • roi_x: float
  • roi_y: float
  • roi_width: float
  • roi_height: float
  • shutter: float
  • gain: float
  • ev: float
  • awb_gain_r: float
  • awb_gain_b: float
  • brightness: float
  • contrast: float
  • saturation: float
  • sharpness: float
  • framerate: float
  • denoise: str
  • info_text: str
  • camera: int

Methods

  • set_metering(mode: MeteringModes) -> None
  • set_white_balance(mode: WhiteBalanceModes) -> None
  • set_exposure_mode(mode: ExposureModes) -> None
  • get_exposure_mode() -> int
  • get_metering_mode() -> int
  • get_white_balance() -> int
  • print() -> None

The three setters update the corresponding native mode setting. The getters return integer mode values. print() prints native option information. timeout is milliseconds; dimensions are pixels; framerate is frames per second.

docs.title: PiCamera
docs.text:
PiCamera() constructs a camera. Its read-only options: Options property exposes the fields above. Important effective constructor defaults are:

Option Default Photo dimensions 3280 × 2464 Video dimensions 640 × 480 framerate 30 timeout 1000 ms Metering MeteringModes.METERING_MATRIX Exposure ExposureModes.EXPOSURE_NORMAL White balance WhiteBalanceModes.WB_AUTO denoise "auto" contrast, saturation, sharpness 1.0 brightness, shutter, gain, ev 0.0 ROI coordinates/dimensions and AWB gains 0.0 camera 0 verbose False

Other fields have no promised default here. Example-selected values are not constructor defaults.

Methods

  • start_photo() -> bool
  • capture_photo() -> Optional[numpy.ndarray]
  • stop_photo() -> bool
  • start_video() -> bool
  • get_video_frame(timeout_ms: int = 1500) -> Optional[numpy.ndarray]
  • stop_video() -> None
  • apply_zoom_options() -> None
  • set_exposure(value: float) -> None
  • set_awb_enable(enable: bool) -> None

start_photo() and start_video() report whether startup succeeded. Use capture_photo() only after photo startup and get_video_frame() after video startup. stop_photo() returns a boolean, whereas stop_video() returns None. Keep explicit cleanup, including when capture or application processing fails. apply_zoom_options() applies the configured ROI; set_exposure(value) and set_awb_enable(enable) forward the native controls. There is no blanket promise that configuration/capture failures are converted into status results: native exceptions may propagate. Releasing the GIL during native calls does not imply that callers may safely mutate configuration concurrently.

docs.title: Frame results and ownership
docs.text:
Capture failure or an empty native frame returns None. Supported successful frames are independent Python-owned NumPy arrays with uint8 storage:

  • Grayscale: (height, width).
  • Three/four channels: (height, width, channels).

The adapter copies rows, including from non-contiguous native storage; keeping an array does not retain a borrowed native frame buffer. An unexpected native channel count returns an empty NumPy array, so non-None alone does not guarantee a usable image. The adapter preserves native channel ordering.

get_video_frame(timeout_ms=1500) uses milliseconds and an unsigned integer timeout. That default is separate from options.timeout.

Only the classes, fields and methods listed here are exposed. Internal LibcameraApp types, native-only controls/fields and explicit destructor APIs are not supported Python interfaces. There is no camera context-manager API.

docs.title: DriveEventListener
docs.text:
DriveEventListener() constructs the listener base. Subclass it and register it with add_listener() to receive events.

Methods

  • on_drive_complete(id: int) -> None
  • Called when a drive command completes successfully.
  • on_drive_error(id: int, side: DriveMotorSide, type: DriveErrorType) -> None
  • Called when a drive operation reports an error.
  • on_drive_state_change(drive_type: DriveType, state: DriveState) -> None
  • Called when the state of a drive operation changes.

The proxy also recognizes legacy Python overrides onDriveComplete, onDriveError and onDriveStateChange. Override-name selection occurs once at registration. These aliases are not additional bound base-class methods; prefer the snake_case methods above.

docs.title: add_listener(listener: Optional[DriveEventListener], priority: bool = False) -> None
docs.text:
Register a listener object to receive events. None does nothing. The wrapper retains the Python target until removal, clearing or accepted disposal.

  • listener: An instance of DriveEventListener or a subclass, or None.
  • priority: Insert with priority ordering (default False).

Repeated registration of the same object is ignored. See callback ordering and lifetime.

docs.title: remove_listener(listener: DriveEventListener) -> None
docs.text: Unregister the object's registration. listener is the Python object previously passed to add_listener(). Removal does not wait for already executing callbacks to finish.

docs.title: init(imu_off_gx: int = 0, imu_off_gy: int = 0, imu_off_gz: int = 0, imu_off_ax: int = 0, imu_off_ay: int = 0, imu_off_az: int = 0) -> int
docs.text:
Initialize the drive control module.

IMU offsets are calibration values stored by the platform. They apply only when the IMU is inactive and at least one supplied gyro offset is nonzero; an already-active IMU keeps its offsets. See IMU initialization for the offset conditions and units.

Parameters

  • imu_off_gx: IMU gyro X offset (calibration). (default: 0)
  • imu_off_gy: IMU gyro Y offset (calibration). (default: 0)
  • imu_off_gz: IMU gyro Z offset (calibration). (default: 0)
  • imu_off_ax: IMU accel X offset (calibration). (default: 0)
  • imu_off_ay: IMU accel Y offset (calibration). (default: 0)
  • imu_off_az: IMU accel Z offset (calibration). (default: 0)

Returns

  • int:
Status code: - 0 : success - 1 : already active / already initialized - -1 : motor setup failed - -2 : IMU init failed

docs.title: dispose(dispose_IMU: bool) -> None
docs.text:
Dispose/shutdown the drive module and release resources.

  • dispose_IMU: Required boolean, with no default. True also requests native IMU shutdown; Python IMU registrations are not cleared as a side effect.

Python returns None, not the native integer status. Native 0/1 permit Drive callback cleanup; native -1 retains surviving registrations. Rejected native outcomes are reported to stderr. From a wrapper callback, this function returns None immediately without cleanup. A None result is not proof of shutdown.

docs.title: is_active() -> bool
docs.text:

Returns

  • bool:
true if active, false otherwise.

docs.title: abort() -> None
docs.text: Request cancellation of the current drive operation. This call may wait for previous work to stop; it does not provide an immediate emergency-stop guarantee. Completion/error events may still be emitted.

docs.title: free_drive(speed: int, is_left: bool, to_forward: bool) -> bool
docs.text:
Manual motor drive (low-level).

Parameters

  • speed: Motor speed percent (0..100); zero stops the selected motor.
  • is_left: True = left motor, False = right motor.
  • to_forward: True = forward, False = backward.

Returns

  • bool:
true if accepted.

Notes

  • Directly update the selected motor. Replacing autonomous work may wait for it to stop.

docs.title: go_xy(id: int, x: int, y: int, speed: int, to_forward: bool, with_brake: bool = False, acceleration_interval: int = 0, control_speed: bool = False, control_force: bool = True) -> bool
docs.text:
Autonomous drive to an (x, y) target (high-level).

docs.title: Image ownership and restrictions
docs.text:
Use VContent for raw image assignment. Initialize Eye before image assignment/position rendering and use idle processing for raw assignments, iris-position reads/rendering, and attached-image frame replacement/active-frame index reads. Python callers share a mutex; callback callers try-lock and raise RuntimeError when busy rather than blocking. Preset and animation operations retain native replacement/cancellation behavior, not a worker-join guarantee.

All assigned images require nonempty frames, a valid active-frame index, converted 12-bit color metadata, and exact frame lengths. RGB channels must each be 0..15; alpha, where present, remains 0..255. Each channel occupies a separate byte:

Slot Dimensions Channels Background Exactly 240×240 RGB Top/bottom lid Width 240, height 1–240 RGBA Iris At least 2×2 RGBA

For each frame the byte count must equal width × height × channel count. Validation checks metadata, dimensions, channel layout, active-frame index, and frame lengths. It does not inspect individual RGB channel values; maintaining the required values is the caller's responsibility. None or invalid structural properties raise ValueError before native indexing. Eye retains native shared ownership for each slot/side; dropping Python references does not free attached content. Replacement retains old owners through the native call. If assignment fails with uncertain native ownership, old and new owners remain retained and subsequent guarded Eye operations raise RuntimeError. Stop image operations after such a failure.

Final image owners remain resident because there is no supported detach-and-join API. Callback disposal never releases them. Preset changes may conservatively retain previous owners, which remain protected from mutation while processing. Do not mutate attached images during active processing or through external C++ callers. Do not operate LCD and Eye concurrently.

Natural animation completion is preferred before image changes. A false is_animating() result, Abort, and wrapper mutexes are not a native join or complete shutdown proof. Native render-busy checks, cancellation and shutdown races remain limitations; wrapper coordination covers Python callers, not native workers or external C++ users.

init(), abort() and set_animation() raise RuntimeError from any wrapper callback. Schedule these on the application control thread. dispose() is callback-only as described above; it is not renderer shutdown. The usual callback replacement, resident proxy and unraisable-exception limitations apply.

See initialization and disposal for component-local cleanup, retained native proxies and interpreter limitations.

  • gx: Gyroscope X offset in millidegrees per second (mdps). (default: 0)
  • gy: Gyroscope Y offset in millidegrees per second (mdps). (default: 0)
  • gz: Gyroscope Z offset in millidegrees per second (mdps). (default: 0)

init() and calculate_offsets() raise RuntimeError from any wrapper callback. dispose() instead returns -1 there. docs.title: Buffer requirements and device ownership
docs.text:
write_lcd and to_lcd_buffer accept buffer-protocol objects, such as bytes, bytearray, compatible memoryview objects and contiguous NumPy byte arrays. There is no SDK Buffer class. Element size must be one byte with buffer format B, b or c. Storage must be C-contiguous and at least the required length; strided views and arbitrary numeric arrays are not accepted. Conversion interprets the contiguous input as a 240×240 RGB/RGBA layout; a particular array shape is not required if the byte layout and size are correct.

Layout Required bytes 240×240 RGB conversion input 172,800 240×240 RGBA conversion input 230,400 Native 12-bit LCD output 86,400 Native 18-bit LCD output 172,800

Use get_buffer_size() for the actual native output requirement. Conversion allocates that output size. Wrong element format raises TypeError; non-contiguous, undersized, overflowing buffers or invalid native size/layout raise ValueError. to_lcd_buffer() and get_color_depth() raise RuntimeError before initialization. A correctly sized buffer does not turn native device failures into Python validation errors.

Initialize before LCD device operations and dispose on the application control thread. Buffer exports remain alive through synchronous native access, with the GIL held. External native threads must not mutate storage or change LCD driver configuration during use. Do not operate LCD and Eye concurrently. Native driver failures, including unchecked depth ioctl results, remain limitations; buffer validation is not a driver-safety guarantee.

docs.title: VContent
docs.text:
VContent() creates empty content with native shared ownership.

Read-only metadata

  • active_frame_id: int: Current active-frame index; read-only from Python.
  • ft: int: Total frames in sequence.
  • width: int: Frame width.
  • height: int: Frame height.
  • path: str: Source path.
  • alpha: bool: True if content has alpha channel.
  • color12Bit: bool: True if content uses converted 12-bit color.
  • ratio: int: Frame-rate divider (for example, 2 divides the base frame rate by two).
  • loop: int: Loop count (0 = forever).
  • frame_count: int: Actual number of stored frames (len(frames)).

Frames property

frames reads as list[list[int]], with each inner list containing byte values 0–255. Reading it returns converted copies, not a live view of native storage. Editing a returned list does not modify native frames: assign the complete replacement through content.frames = replacement. Assignment does not update read-only metadata or readiness. frame_count reflects the stored vector size; ft remains the loaded sequence metadata.

Methods

  • __init__() -> None
  • Create an empty VContent.
  • is_ready() -> bool
  • Return True if the content has been loaded successfully.
  • get_frame_bytes(index: int = 0) -> bytes
  • Return an independent bytes copy of the stored RGB/RGBA frame. An index outside the stored frame vector raises IndexError; negative integers fail unsigned-index conversion.
  • get_image(path: str, isRGBA: bool, set12Bit: bool) -> VContent
  • Static method. Load a PNG from path and return content. All three arguments are required. isRGBA selects RGBA (True) or RGB (False) output; set12Bit requests 12-bit color conversion: each RGB channel is divided by 16 to yield 0..15; alpha remains unchanged at 0..255. Channels still occupy separate bytes, so conversion does not change the buffer length. Loading/decoding failure produces unready content; check is_ready() rather than assuming a missing file raises FileNotFoundError.

docs.title: Eye ownership and restrictions
docs.text:
See Eye image requirements. Eye retains a native shared owner for every assigned slot/side, so deleting a Python reference does not free an image still attached to Eye. Final owners remain resident because there is no supported native detach-and-join API; Eye callback disposal does not release them.

Replacing frames on attached content requires idle Eye processing. Validation checks role, dimensions, channel layout, active-frame index, converted-color metadata, and every frame's byte length. It does not check individual RGB values: the caller must keep RGB in 0..15 and alpha in 0..255 for converted Eye content. Invalid structural properties or metadata raise ValueError. Reading active_frame_id on attached content also requires idle Eye processing. Busy or uncertain ownership state raises RuntimeError; callback callers use a nonblocking lock attempt. These guards do not synchronize external native callers. Do not mutate attached content through C++ while using Python wrappers.

Standalone frame assignment is not an image-loading or metadata-update operation.

docs.text:
Below is the module’s examples/python/ArmControl/example.py as a starting point.

"""
example.py

This example shows how to implement an event listener in Python
(similar to `class MyListener : public ArmEventListener` in C++) and use it
with the ArmControl API.

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the arm controller
- Creating a listener class by inheriting from ArmEventListener
- Registering the listener instance (non-static / object-based)
- Sending a movement command using set_angle()
- Reading back the current angle(s)
- Cleaning up (dispose)

The wrapper retains registered Python listeners. This example also keeps a local
reference; component disposal owns callback cleanup.
"""


import time
import doly_arm as arm
import doly_helper as helper


class MyListener(arm.ArmEventListener):
    def onArmComplete(self, id, side):
        print("[info] complete", id, side)

    def onArmError(self, id, side, errorType):
        print("[error] error", id, side, errorType)

    def onArmStateChange(self, side, state):
        print("[info] state", side, state)

    def onArmMovement(self, side, degreeChange):
        print("[info] move", side, degreeChange)


def main():

    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] ArmControl Version: {arm.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass


    # *** IMPORTANT ***
    # Read settings for servo calibration data, otherwise arm control won't work.
    # one time read is sufficient for the lifetime of the application
    if helper.read_settings() < 0:
        print("[error] Read settings failed")
        return -2

    # Initialize ArmControl
    rc = arm.init()
    if rc < 0:
        print(f"[error] ArmControl.init failed rc={rc}")
        return -2

    result = 0
    try:
        # add event listener
        listener = MyListener()
        arm.add_listener(listener, priority=False)


        # Example command
        cmd_id = 1
        rc = arm.set_angle(cmd_id, arm.ArmSide.Both, speed=30, angle=90, with_brake=False)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] set_angle failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # Wait until done (simple polling example)
        while True:
            state = arm.get_state(arm.ArmSide.Both)
            if state == arm.ArmState.Error:
                print("[error] Arm movement ended in Error")
                return -3
            if state == arm.ArmState.Completed:
                break
            time.sleep(0.05)

        angles = arm.get_current_angle(arm.ArmSide.Both)
        for a in angles:
            print(f"angle: side={a.side} angle={a.angle}")
    finally:
        # Cleanup stays on the control thread; preserve any original exception.
        try:
            cleanup_rc = arm.dispose()
            if cleanup_rc < 0:
                print(f"[error] arm.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                result = 1
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] arm.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1
    time.sleep(0.2)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.text:
Below is the module’s examples/python/BatteryControl/example.py as a starting point.

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the battery controller
- Registering the static event listener
- Reading the battery information
- Cleaning up

"""


import time
import doly_battery as battery


def on_alarm(capacity:int):
    print(f"[info] Battery Alarm! capacity={capacity}")


def main():
    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] BatteryControl Version: {battery.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass


    result = 0
    initialized = False
    registered = []
    try:
        # Register static event listeners
        battery.on_alarm(on_alarm)
        registered.append(battery.on_alarm)

        # Initialize BatteryControl
        rc = battery.init()
        if rc < 0:
            print("[error] BatteryControl init failed")
            return -2
        initialized = True

        # Get battery capacity after a short delay following initialization.
        time.sleep(0.5)
        val = battery.get_capacity()
        print(f"[info] Battery capacity={val}")

        # Set alarm threshold to 100%, will be trigger at %99
        battery.set_alarm_threshold(100)

        # Wait alarm event
        print("[info] Wait for alarm event for 15 seconds")
        time.sleep(15)

    finally:

import cv2
import doly_camera

def main():
    print("Initializing camera")

    cam = doly_camera.PiCamera()

    cam.options.photo_width = 3280
    cam.options.photo_height = 2464
    cam.options.video_width = 1280
    cam.options.video_height = 960
    cam.options.framerate = 15
    cam.options.verbose = False

    result = 0
    try:
        # -----------------------------
        # Single frame capture example
        # -----------------------------
        if not cam.start_photo():
            print("[error] Camera start_photo failed")
            return -2
        try:
            frame = cam.capture_photo()  # numpy array or None
            if frame is None:
                print("[error] Camera read buffer failed at capture!")
                return -3
            if not cv2.imwrite("capture.jpg", frame):
                print("[error] Saving capture.jpg failed")
                return -3
            print("Frame saved!")
        finally:
            try:
                if not cam.stop_photo():
                    print("[error] Camera stop_photo failed")
                    result = 1
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[error] Camera stop_photo raised: {exc}")
                result = 1
        if result:
            return result

        # -----------------------------
        # Video frame capture example
        #
        # This example uses an OpenCV imshow() window to display captured frames. (X11 forwarding over SSH)
        # However, you have several options to view the camera output.
        # Here are a few examples:
        # 1) Stream frames over the network (probably fast and best option, requires addditional coding)
        #        inside your capture loop:
        #        std::vector<uchar> jpeg;
        #        cv::imencode(".jpg", frame, jpeg); (optional: reduce JPEG quality for small data)
        #        -> send jpeg over socket / HTTP
        # 2) X11 forwarding over SSH (simple, but slow)
        #
        #
        # This example uses an OpenCV imshow() window to display captured frames (X11 forwarding over SSH).
        #
        # Note:
        # - The image window may NOT be displayed when running with root privileges
        #   (this can cause GTK/X11 permission errors).
        # - X11 forwarding is required to display the window over SSH.
        # - Make sure your SSH client supports X11 forwarding.
        #
        # To test whether X11 forwarding is working correctly:
        #   sudo apt install -y x11-apps
        #   xclock
        # If X11 is working, a clock window should appear.
        # These historical setup suggestions require separate authorization;
        # this example does not install dependencies or configure X11.
        #
        # Also verify that DISPLAY is set:
        #   echo $DISPLAY
        # It should show something like "localhost:11.0"
        # -----------------------------
        if not cam.start_video():
            print("[error] Camera start_video failed")
            return -4
        try:
            print("Video window is live! Press ESC to quit!")

            cv2.namedWindow("Camera", cv2.WINDOW_NORMAL)
            cv2.resizeWindow("Camera", 640, 480)

            time_out_ms = 1500
            total_frame = 300 #test frame count

            while total_frame > 0:
                total_frame -= 1

                frame = cam.get_video_frame(time_out_ms)  # numpy array or None
                if frame is not None:
                    # resize frame for fast X11 transfer
                    resized = cv2.resize(frame, (640, 480), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
                    cv2.imshow("Camera", resized)
                    k = cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF
                    if k == 27:  # ESC
                        break
                else:
                    print("[warn] getVideoFrame() timeout/fail")

        finally:
            try:
                cam.stop_video()  # Returns None.
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[error] Camera stop_video raised: {exc}")
                result = 1
    finally:
        try:
            cv2.destroyAllWindows()
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] Window cleanup raised: {exc}")
            result = 1

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the drive controller
- Registering the static event listener
- Sending drive commands using multiple options
- Reading the current estimated position
- Cleaning up

"""


import time
import doly_drive as drive


def on_drive_complete(cmd_id: int):
    print(f"[info] Drive complete id={cmd_id}")


def on_drive_error(cmd_id: int, side, err_type):
    # side is DriveMotorSide enum, err_type is DriveErrorType enum
    print(f"[error] Drive error id={cmd_id} side={int(side)} type={int(err_type)}")


def on_drive_state_change(drive_type, state):
    print(f"[info] Drive state type={int(drive_type)} state={int(state)}")


def main():
    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] DriveControl Version: {drive.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass


    result = 0
    initialized = False
    registered = []
    try:
        # Register static event listeners
        drive.on_complete(on_drive_complete)
        registered.append(drive.on_complete)
        drive.on_error(on_drive_error)
        registered.append(drive.on_error)
        drive.on_state_change(on_drive_state_change)
        registered.append(drive.on_state_change)

        # Initialize DriveControl with zero IMU offsets (example)
        # For better performance provide actual calibrated IMU offsets.
        # Check ../Helper/example.py for more information
        rc = drive.init()
        if rc < 0:
            print("[error] DriveControl init failed")
            return -2
        initialized = True

        speed = 50  # example speed % (0..100)

        # Example 1: go 100mm forward, brake at end
        if not drive.go_distance(1, 100, speed, True, True):
            print("[error] Drive distance command rejected")
            return -3

        # Example 2: Rotate 45 degrees counterclockwise on wheel, with brake at end
        # drive.go_rotate(2, -45.0, False, speed, True, True)

        # Example 3: Go to X= -100mm, Y= 200mm, approaching forward with acceleration, without brake at end
        # drive.go_xy(1, -100, 200, speed, True, False, 50)

        # Example 4: Free drive left and right wheels forward at specified speed for 2 seconds
        # drive.free_drive(speed, False, True)  # Low-level drive right
        # drive.free_drive(speed, True, True)   # Low-level drive left
        # time.sleep(2.0)
        # Stop driving wheels
        # drive.free_drive(0, False, True)
        # drive.free_drive(0, True, True)

        # Wait until done (simple polling example)
        while True:
            state = drive.get_state()
            if state != drive.DriveState.Running:
                break
            time.sleep(0.05)
        if state == drive.DriveState.Error:
            print("[error] Drive movement ended in Error")
            return -3

        # Get final position
        pos = drive.get_position()
        print(f"[info] Robot pos x={pos.x} y={pos.y} head={pos.head}")
    finally:
        if initialized:
            # Also disposes native IMU. The None adapter cannot prove cleanup success.
            try:
                drive.dispose(True)
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[error] drive.dispose raised: {exc}")
                result = 1
        else:
            # Initialization failed: remove only registrations installed by this example.
            for unregister in registered:
                try:
                    unregister(None)
                except Exception as exc:
                    print(f"[error] Callback removal raised: {exc}")
                    result = 1

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

from doly_vcontent import VContent

def on_eye_complete(anim_id: int):
    print(f"[info] Eye animation complete id:{anim_id}")


def on_eye_abort(anim_id: int):
    print(f"[warn] Eye animation abort id:{anim_id}")

        print(f"[info] EyeControl Version:{eye.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:

    # Initialize EyeControl
    rc = eye.init(ColorCode.Blue, ColorCode.White)
    if rc < 0:
        print("[error] EyeControl init failed")
        return -2

    result = 0
    try:
        # Register static event listeners
        eye.on_start(on_eye_start)
        eye.on_complete(on_eye_complete)
        eye.on_abort(on_eye_abort)

        time.sleep(3)

        # Example: Change iris
        rc = eye.set_iris(eye.IrisShape.Modern, ColorCode.DarkGreen, eye.EyeSide.Both)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Set iris failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        time.sleep(3)

        # Example: Set Animation (non-blocking)
        rc = eye.set_animation(1, eye.expressions.EXCITED)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Set animation failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # Wait until animation complete (same as while (EyeControl::isAnimating()))
        while eye.is_animating():
            time.sleep(0.01)

        time.sleep(3)

        # Example: Using custom images for lids, iris or background
        visual = VContent.get_image("/.doly/images/lids/11B.png", True, True)

        if not visual.is_ready():
            print("[error] image load failed!")
            return -3
        # Bottom lid. Assignment errors propagate through finally; no further image operations.
        eye.set_lid_image(visual, False, eye.EyeSide.Both)

        # EyeControl::setIrisPosition(EyeSide::BOTH, 120, 120, 1.2, 1.2, 0, 180);
        rc = eye.set_position(eye.EyeSide.Both, 120, 120, 1.2, 1.2, 0, 180)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Set iris position failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # EyeControl::getIrisPosition(EyeSide::LEFT, x, y);
        rc, x, y = eye.get_iris_position(eye.EyeSide.Left)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Get iris position failed rc={rc}")
            return -3
        print(f"[info] Left iris position: {x},{y} (rc={rc})")
    finally:
        # Cleanup stays on the control thread; preserve any original exception.
        try:
            # Callback cleanup only: no renderer shutdown, image release or worker join.
            eye.dispose()
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] eye.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1

    return result

    raise SystemExit(main())

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the LED controller
- Setting static event callbacks
- Change LEDs with fade effect
- Change LEDs instant
- Cleaning up (dispose)

"""

import time
import doly_led as led
from doly_color import Color, ColorCode

def on_led_complete(cmd_id: int, side):
    print(f"[info] Led complete id={cmd_id} side={side}")

def on_led_error(cmd_id: int, side, err_type):
    print(f"[error] Led error id={cmd_id} side={side} error={err_type}")

def main():

    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] LedControl Version: {led.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass



    # Initialize LED controller
    rc = led.init()
    if rc < 0:
        print(f"[error] LedControl.init failed rc={rc}")
        return -2

    result = 0
    try:
        # Register static event listeners if required
        led.on_complete(on_led_complete)
        led.on_error(on_led_error)

        # fade effect example
        activity1 = led.LedActivity()
        activity1.mainColor = Color.from_code(ColorCode.Red)
        activity1.fadeColor = Color.from_code(ColorCode.Blue)
        activity1.fade_time = 2000  # 2 seconds (milliseconds)

        led.process_activity(1, led.LedSide.Both, activity1)
        # Let the activity run for a while on another thread
        time.sleep(2.5)

        # instant color change example
        activity2 = led.LedActivity()
        activity2.mainColor = Color.from_code(ColorCode.Orange)
        activity2.fade_time = 0

        led.process_activity(2, led.LedSide.Right, activity2)

        # wait activity event completion before dispose
        time.sleep(0.2)
    finally:
        # Cleanup stays on the control thread; preserve any original exception.
        try:
            cleanup_rc = led.dispose()
            if cleanup_rc < 0:
                print(f"[error] led.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                result = 1
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] led.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1
    time.sleep(0.2)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the external servo controller (IO plug servos)
- Setting static event callbacks
- Setting servo position
- Releasing servo hold
- Cleaning up (dispose)

"""

import time
import doly_servo as servo

def on_servo_abort(id, channel):
    print(f"[info] Servo abort id:{id} channel:{channel}")

def on_servo_complete(id, channel):
    print(f"[info] Servo complete id:{id} channel:{channel}")

def on_servo_error(id, channel):
    print(f"[error] Servo error id:{id} channel:{channel}")

def main():

    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] ServoControl Version: {servo.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass


    # Initialize servo controler
    rc = servo.init()
    if rc < 0:
        print(f"[error] ServoControl.init failed rc={rc}")
        return -2

    result = 0
    attempted_channels = []
    try:
        # Add static event listeners
        servo.on_complete(on_servo_complete)
        servo.on_abort(on_servo_abort)
        servo.on_error(on_servo_error)

        # Set positions on both external servos
        attempted_channels.append(servo.ServoId.Servo0)
        rc = servo.set_servo(1, servo.ServoId.Servo0, 180, 100, False)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Set Servo0 failed rc={rc}")
            return -3
        attempted_channels.append(servo.ServoId.Servo1)
        rc = servo.set_servo(2, servo.ServoId.Servo1, 90, 1, False)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Set Servo1 failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # Preserve the original dwell; it does not guarantee both servos have completed.
        time.sleep(3)
    finally:
        # Release hold on each attempted channel, including after a partial command failure.
        # Busy (-2) is a failure: do not extend the dwell or add a completion wait.
        for channel in attempted_channels:
            try:
                cleanup_rc = servo.release(channel)
                if cleanup_rc < 0:
                    print(f"[error] Servo release failed channel={channel} rc={cleanup_rc}")
                    result = 1
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[error] Servo release raised channel={channel}: {exc}")
                result = 1
        try:
            cleanup_rc = servo.dispose()
            if cleanup_rc < 0:
                print(f"[error] servo.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                result = 1
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] servo.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1
    time.sleep(0.2)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the ToF sensor controller
- Registering the static event listeners
- Cleaning up (dispose)

"""


import time
import doly_tof as tof

# Event returns TofGesture data for both sides.
def on_proximity_gesture(left, right):
    print(f"[info] Gesture event L={left.type} R={right.type}")

# Event returns TofData information for both sides.
def on_proximity_threshold(left, right):
    print(f"[info] Proximity event range L={left.range_mm} R={right.range_mm}")

def main():

    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] TofControl Version: {tof.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass



    # Initialize ToF sensor controler
    rc = tof.init()
    if rc < 0:
        print(f"[error] TofControl.init failed rc={rc}")
        return -2

    result = 0
    try:
        # Setup continuous ToF control with 50ms interval and proximity threshold 40mm (enabled)
        if tof.setup_continuous(50, 40) < 0:
            print("[error] TofControl setup failed")
            return -3

        # Register static event listeners
        tof.on_proximity_gesture(on_proximity_gesture)
        tof.on_proximity_threshold(on_proximity_threshold)

        # Run for 20 seconds to test TOF events
        print(f"[info] Run for 20 seconds to test TOF sensor events")
        time.sleep(20)

        # Stop continuous reading and disable events
        if tof.setup_continuous(0) < 0:
            print("[error] TofControl setup failed")
            return -4

        # Single read example
        sensors = tof.get_sensors_data()
        for sensor in sensors:
            print(f"[info] Single Read Sensor[{sensor.side}] Range[{sensor.range_mm}mm] Error[{sensor.error}]")
    finally:
        # Cleanup stays on the control thread; preserve any original exception.
        try:
            cleanup_rc = tof.dispose()
            if cleanup_rc < 0:
                print(f"[error] tof.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                result = 1
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] tof.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1
    time.sleep(0.2)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""
example.py

It demonstrates:
- Initializing the TTS (text to speech) controller
- Produce sound
- Initializing the sound controller
- Playing sound
- Cleaning up (dispose)

"""

import time
import doly_sound as snd
import doly_tts as tts

def main():

    # Version
    try:
        print(f"[info] TtsControl Version: {tts.get_version():.3f}")
    except AttributeError:
        pass


    # Initialize tts controler
    print("[info] Initialize and load voice model...")
    rc = tts.init(tts.VoiceModel.Model1, "output.wav")
    if rc < 0:
        print(f"[error] TtsControl.init failed rc={rc}")
        return -2

    result = 0
    sound_initialized = False
    try:
        # Generate speech sound file from text
        print("[info] Produce Text to Speech")
        rc = tts.produce("Hello, this is a text to speech test example.")
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Produce speech failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # Initialize sound controler to test sound file
        rc = snd.init()
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] SoundControl.init failed rc={rc}")
            return -3
        sound_initialized = True

        # Play sound
        rc = snd.play("output.wav", 1)
        if rc < 0:
            print(f"[error] Play failed rc={rc}")
            return -3

        # Preserve the original five-second playback interval; completion is not polled.
        time.sleep(5)
    finally:
        # Preserve TTS-before-Sound cleanup; attempt both even if one fails.
        try:
            cleanup_rc = tts.dispose()
            if cleanup_rc < 0:
                print(f"[error] tts.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                result = 1
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[error] tts.dispose raised: {exc}")
            result = 1
        if sound_initialized:
            try:
                cleanup_rc = snd.dispose()
                if cleanup_rc < 0:
                    print(f"[error] snd.dispose failed rc={cleanup_rc}")
                    result = 1
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[error] snd.dispose raised: {exc}")
                result = 1
    time.sleep(0.2)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.title: Do I need to install anything on the robot?
docs.text: No. The Python SDK is installed with the robot image.

docs.title: Why does my script conflict with the Doly service?
docs.text: If the service and your script try to access the same hardware at the same time, conflicts can happen. Stop the doly.service before running scripts that directly control hardware. Please refer to the SDK examples for a demonstration.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Some modules talk to Linux device nodes (for example, /dev/doly_lcd) or sysfs entries. If a module works as root but not as a user, it is usually a permissions problem. We have already added the doly user to the custom doly group. If you plan to add a new user to your system to interact with Linux device nodes, please follow the instructions below.

docs.title: Recommended approach
docs.text:
• Use udev rules to assign a group and permissions to Doly devices
  • Add your user to the appropriate group (often video, dialout, or a custom doly group)
